claim: NmMetQ is a substrate-binding protein (SBP) from Neisseria meningitidis that has been identified as a surface-exposed candidate antigen for meningococcal vaccines.
source: NmMetQ is a substrate-binding protein (SBP) from Neisseria meningitidis that has been identified as a surface-exposed candidate antigen for meningococcal vaccines.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pizza et al., 2000 in the introduction section

claim: The surface location of NmMetQ challenges the prevailing view that SBPs in Gram-negative bacteria are localized to the periplasmic space.
source: However, this location for NmMetQ challenges the prevailing view that SBPs in Gram-negative bacteria are localized to the periplasmic space to promote interaction with their cognate ABC transporter embedded in the bacterial inner membrane.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SBP localization and inference from the observed surface localization of NmMetQ

claim: NmMetQ is a lipoprotein (lipo-NmMetQ) that binds multiple methionine analogs.
source: Here, we show that NmMetQ is a lipoprotein (lipo-NmMetQ) that binds multiple methionine analogs and stimulates the ATPase activity of NmMetNI.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing lipid modifications and FAXS experiments showing binding to methionine analogs

claim: Lipo-NmMetQ stimulates the ATPase activity of NmMetNI.
source: Here, we show that NmMetQ is a lipoprotein (lipo-NmMetQ) that binds multiple methionine analogs and stimulates the ATPase activity of NmMetNI.
evidence: Supported by ATPase activity assays showing increased activity in the presence of lipo-NmMetQ and L-methionine

claim: The structures of NmMetNI were determined in the presence and absence of lipo-NmMetQ using single-particle electron cryo-microscopy.
source: Using single-particle electron cryo-microscopy, we determined the structures of NmMetNI in the presence and absence of lipo-NmMetQ.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM data collection and structure determination described in the manuscript

claim: NmMetQ tethers to membranes via a lipid anchor and has dual function and localization, playing a role in NmMetNI-mediated transport at the inner membrane and moonlighting on the bacterial surface.
source: Based on our data, we propose that NmMetQ tethers to membranes via a lipid anchor and has dual function and localization, playing a role in NmMetNI-mediated transport at the inner membrane and moonlighting on the bacterial surface.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing lipid modification, ATPase stimulation, and previous reports of surface localization

claim: NmMetQ has been shown to interact with human brain microvascular endothelial cells, potentially acting as an adhesin.

claim: SBPs reside in the periplasm of Gram-negative bacteria, binding and delivering molecules to cognate ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporters in the inner membrane.

claim: The ABC transporter-dependent role of SBPs has been well characterized for multiple ABC transporter systems.

source: These results suggest that modifications to both the amino group and stereochemistry lead to significantly weaker binding than the singly modified derivative.
evidence: Based on inference from FAXS experimental data

claim: L-methioninol failed to displace the reporter molecule in FAXS experiments.
source: Specifically, L-methioninol, with the carboxyl group reduced to an alcohol, failed to displace the reporter molecule while L-methionine ethyl ester only partially displaced the reporter molecule (Figure 3C, circles).
evidence: Supported by FAXS experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: L-methionine ethyl ester only partially displaced the reporter molecule in FAXS experiments.
source: Specifically, L-methioninol, with the carboxyl group reduced to an alcohol, failed to displace the reporter molecule while L-methionine ethyl ester only partially displaced the reporter molecule (Figure 3C, circles).
evidence: Supported by FAXS experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Seleno-L-methionine, L-methionine sulfoximine, and L-norleucine were well tolerated, with a greater displacement of the reporter molecule than D-methionine in FAXS experiments.
source: Methionine analogs with changes to the sulfur atom, including seleno-L-methionine, L-methionine sulfoximine, and L-norleucine were well tolerated, with a greater displacement of the reporter molecule than D-methionine, which has an estimated Kd of 3.5 μM (Nguyen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by FAXS experimental data and citation to Nguyen et al., 2019

claim: L-ornithine failed to displace the reporter molecule in FAXS experiments.
source: However, L-ornithine failed to displace the reporter molecule, suggesting that binding of ligands with a charged amino group is energetically unfavorable.
evidence: Supported by FAXS experimental data

claim: Binding of ligands with a charged amino group is energetically unfavorable for NLM-NmMetQ.
source: However, L-ornithine failed to displace the reporter molecule, suggesting that binding of ligands with a charged amino group is energetically unfavorable.
evidence: Based on inference from FAXS experimental data

claim: Increasing the side-chain length by an addition of a methylene group (L-ethionine) was better tolerated than decreasing the length by one carbon (S-methyl-L-cysteine).
source: Side-chain length also plays a role in methionine analog affinity to NLM-NmMetQ. Increasing the side-chain length by an addition of a methylene group (L-ethionine) was better tolerated than decreasing the length by one carbon (S-methyl-L-cysteine).
evidence: Supported by FAXS experimental data

claim: Shorter thiol derivatives (L-cysteine and L-homocysteine) were ineffective at displacing the reporter molecule in FAXS experiments.
source: Shorter thiol derivatives (L-cysteine and L-homocysteine) were ineffective at displacing the reporter molecule.
evidence: Supported by FAXS experimental data

claim: NLM-NmMetQ can accommodate variability in the binding of methionine analogs, including modifications to the amino group, D-stereochemistry, and changes in the side-chain (to a limited extent), while exhibiting little tolerance for variations in the carboxyl group.
source: Together, our data establish that NLM-NmMetQ can accommodate variability in the binding of methionine analogs, including modifications to the amino group, D-stereochemistry, and changes in the side-chain (to a limited extent), while exhibiting little tolerance for variations in the carboxyl group.
evidence: Based on inference from FAXS experimental data

claim: N-acetyl-L-methionine, N-formyl-L-methionine, L-norleucine, L-ethionine, and L-methionine sulfoximine led to substrate-stimulated ATPase activity.

claim: No correlation was seen between affinity to NLM-NmMetQ and NmMetNI stimulation.
source: However, no correlation was seen between affinity to NLM-NmMetQ and NmMetNI stimulation.
evidence: Based on comparison of FAXS and ATPase activity data

claim: Binding to NmMetQ is necessary to initiate transport; however, this step alone does not determine the magnitude of NmMetNI ATPase stimulation.
source: This data suggest that binding to NmMetQ is necessary to initiate transport; however, this step alone does not determine the magnitude of NmMetNI ATPase stimulation.
evidence: Based on inference from FAXS and ATPase activity data

claim: With 1 mM AMPPNP, the structural analysis of an equimolar mixture of lipo-NmMetQ and NmMetNI revealed that NmMetNI was captured in the inward-facing conformation at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: With 1 mM AMPPNP (below the Km), the structural analysis of an equimolar mixture of lipo-NmMetQ and NmMetNI revealed that NmMetNI was captured in the inward-facing conformation at 3.3 Å resolution (Figure 4A); no densities for either AMPPNP and lipo-NmMetQ were observed.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure determination shown in Figure 4A

claim: No densities for either AMPPNP and lipo-NmMetQ were observed in the 3.3 Å resolution structure of NmMetNI.
source: With 1 mM AMPPNP (below the Km), the structural analysis of an equimolar mixture of lipo-NmMetQ and NmMetNI revealed that NmMetNI was captured in the inward-facing conformation at 3.3 Å resolution (Figure 4A); no densities for either AMPPNP and lipo-NmMetQ were observed.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: The overall architecture of NmMetNI is similar to previously determined structures of EcMetNI, comprising two copies of each TMD and NBD, encoded by MetI and MetN, respectively.
source: The overall architecture of NmMetNI is similar to previously determined structures of EcMetNI, comprising two copies of each TMD and NBD, encoded by MetI and MetN, respectively (Kadaba et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2012).

claim: Each MetI subunit contains five transmembrane helices per monomer for a total of ten transmembrane helices per transporter.
source: Each MetI subunit contains five transmembrane helices per monomer for a total of ten transmembrane helices per transporter (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4B

claim: NmMetNI and EcMetNI have similar subunit folds, with the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 2.4 Å over 843 Cα atoms.
source: A comparison between NmMetNI and EcMetNI reveals similar subunit folds, with the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 2.4 Å over 843 Cα atoms.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison

claim: The NmMetN subunits lack the C2 autoinhibitory domain.
source: As predicted from the primary sequence, the NmMetN subunits lack the C2 autoinhibitory domain.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and sequence comparison

claim: In the inward-facing conformation of NmMetNI, the NBDs interact directly.
source: In the inward-facing conformation of NmMetNI, the NBDs interact directly.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure

claim: Type I ABC importers share a common quaternary arrangement in the inward-facing conformation such that the presence of a regulatory domain increases the separation of the NBD:NBD distance in comparison to the homologous structure without a regulatory domain.
source: A comparison of these structures suggests that type I ABC importers share a common quaternary arrangement in the inward-facing conformation such that the presence of a regulatory domain increases the separation of the NBD:NBD distance in comparison to the homologous structure without a regulatory domain Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.
evidence: Based on inference from structural comparisons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: The structure of the lipo-NmMetQ:NmMetNI complex was determined to 6.4 Å resolution in the presence of 5 mM ATP.
source: Reasoning that increasing the nucleotide concentration to above the Km for MgATP would promote complex formation, we mixed equimolar lipo-NmMetQ and NmMetQ in the presence of 5 mM ATP. Under these conditions, we were able to determine the single-particle cryo-EM structure of the complex to 6.4 Å resolution (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure determination shown in Figure 4

claim: The structure shows lipo-NmMetQ docked onto the NmMetI subunits and the NmMetN subunits in a closed dimer state.
source: Our model shows lipo-NmMetQ docked onto the NmMetI subunits and the NmMetN subunits in a closed dimer state.

claim: No clear density was seen for the lipid moiety of lipo-NmMetQ or ATP in the 6.4 Å resolution structure.
source: No clear density was seen for the lipid moiety of lipo-NmMetQ or ATP (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Liu et. al. were not able to observe the lipid moiety of lipo-SBP in complex with an ABC transporter, despite these cryo-EM structures resolving at higher resolutions (3.30, 3.44, 3.78 Å).
source: Of note, Liu et. al. were also not able to observe the lipid moiety of lipo-SBP in complex with an ABC transporter, despite these cryo-EM structures resolving at higher resolutions (3.30, 3.44, 3.78 Å) Liu et al., 2020.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020

claim: NmMetNI and EcMetNI in the outward-facing conformation in complex with their respective MetQ proteins have similar conformations, with RMSD of 2.2 Å over 1048 Cα atoms.

claim: In the outward-facing conformation, the NBD:NBD arrangement is similar for both EcMetNI and NmMetNI.

claim: Lipid-modified MetQ proteins may be present in all classes of Proteobacteria (Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Epsilon).
source: Our data revealed that lipid-modified MetQ proteins may be present in all classes of Proteobacteria (Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Epsilon), with varying number of lipid-modified MetQ proteins in each Order (magenta vs white).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis using SignalP 5.0

claim: Lipid modification of MetQ proteins are likely present in a wide variety of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: These results suggest that lipid modification of MetQ proteins are not restricted to N. meningitidis(this work) and E. coli (Tokuda et al., 2007; Carlson et al., 2019) and are likely present in a wide variety of Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: Based on inference from bioinformatics analysis and citations to Tokuda et al., 2007 and Carlson et al., 2019

claim: At the IM, lipo-NmMetQ plays a role in nutrient acquisition.
source: In our model, NmMetQ is a lipoprotein with dual function and localization (Figure 6). At the IM, lipo-NmMetQ plays a role in nutrient acquisition.

source: Lipo-NmMetQ is then transported to the OM, possibly through the localization of the lipoprotein system (Lol) (Zückert, 2014), and then flipped to the surface of the cell via Slam (a protein involved in lipoprotein surface exposure in N. meningitidis) (Hooda et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on speculation and citations to Zückert, 2014 and Hooda et al., 2016

claim: Lipo-NmMetQ is flipped to the surface of the cell via Slam (a protein involved in lipoprotein surface exposure in N. meningitidis).
source: Lipo-NmMetQ is then transported to the OM, possibly through the localization of the lipoprotein system (Lol) (Zückert, 2014), and then flipped to the surface of the cell via Slam (a protein involved in lipoprotein surface exposure in N. meningitidis) (Hooda et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on speculation and citation to Hooda et al., 2016

claim: The lipid modifications are central to the model, helping to explain how NmMetQ remains at the surface of the bacterium.

claim: E. coli has successfully expressed lipoproteins with their native signal sequences from other Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Since previous studies have successfully expressed in E. coli lipoproteins with their native signal sequences from other Gram-negative bacteria (Parra et al., 2010; Hooda et al., 2016), including two lipoproteins from N. meningitidis (Fantappiè et al., 2017), we reasoned that these biochemical pathways are sufficiently similar between E. coli and N. meningitidis to justify this assumption.
evidence: Supported by citations to Parra et al., 2010, Hooda et al., 2016, and Fantappiè et al., 2017

claim: Lipo-NmMetQ binds to the TMDs of NmMetNI, similar to what is observed with the well-characterized E. coli ABC methionine transporter system, EcMetQ:EcMetNI.

evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure and citation to Nguyen et al., 2018

claim: Methionine is a scarce amino acid in human nasopharynx, where N. meningitidis primarily colonizes.
source: Given that methionine is a scarce amino acid in human nasopharynx (Krismer et al., 2014), where N. meningitidis primarily colonizes (Stephens et al., 2007), and one of the most expensive amino acids to synthesize in terms of ATP requirement (as measured in E. coli) (Kaleta et al., 2013), having multiple copies of NmMetQ may enable N. meningitidis to more efficiently capture methionine from the nutrient-limited environment.
evidence: Supported by citations to Krismer et al., 2014 and Stephens et al., 2007

claim: Methionine is one of the most expensive amino acids to synthesize in terms of ATP requirement (as measured in E. coli).

claim: Having multiple copies of NmMetQ may enable N. meningitidis to more efficiently capture methionine from the nutrient-limited environment.
